Here is a copilot-generated summary:

ZEN University’s ZEN Mathematics Center announced LANA, a long‑running formalization project aimed at (1) developing a Lean library for key theorems in anabelian geometry and (2) neutrally verifying Mochizuki’s Inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT) through formalization. The team reports major progress in understanding IUT but identifies a critical unresolved point in the passage from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12, which they can now precisely formulate but not yet resolve—leaving open whether it reflects a genuine gap or a remaining limitation in human understanding.
Kim's gist link above has an English summary at the top (which broadly agrees with Damiano's copilot summary) and now has an English translation as well.
Happy to answer questions, although I will be afk for an hour now.

Announcement post:
https://zen.ac.jp/en/zmc/topics/jwz-o8xr3v6f
Just watched the video and the article is an accurate transcript of the announcement (excluding Q&A)
The summary Damiano posted is quite accurate! I’m also happy to answer any questions.

Is there a plan to produce something like a blueprint for the theory up to Theorem 3.11, or at least a document that more closely conforms to common mathematical narrative conventions than what we have seen to date?
@Scott Carnahan the current plan is to release various mathematical artifacts this summer (July).
Looking at their 2018 paper, the issue brought up by Scholze and Stix was also in Corollary 3.12. Is the “critical point” you have come to the same as the one they wrote about?

Great question!

The "critical point" we encountered is indeed in a similar location as the one brought up by Scholze and Stix. However there are several subtle differences between what we encountered and what Scholze and Stix point out, and we want to make sure we can be completely precise before making any claims. As we mentioned during the press conference, we plan to explain all of these subtleties this summer.

@Brian Nugent It should be remembered that Scholze and Stix were open in saying they were working with some approximation of the full theory, and that they believed that what they identified was also a problem in the actual paper. Mochizuki's contention was that their approximation lost too much fidelity, but his counter-arguments were not enough to convince Scholze and Stix that they were making a crucial error in their analysis.

It was an exercise in 'post-rigorous mathematics' in the sense of @Terence Tao , so one expects that roadbumps identified in the formalisation may well be "subtly different", as Adam put it.

How do you think this will relate to the Mochizuki-lead Lean efforts? I assume there was no collaboration given it wasn’t mentioned. Do you think this will make Mochizuki’s effort’s easier, either because they will have your version to start from or (if they want to do it differently) will have your version as a reference?

@Jason Rute :

Our team (project LANA) is indeed independent from Mochizuki, but we have been communicating with him in an attempt to get clarification on the "critical point" mentioned above. While we're not collaborating with Mochizuki directly in our project, Lean has actually been used as part of our communication with him. For example, we have sent him a short Lean file containing axioms as placeholders for various key objects of IUT, and a statement indicating the critical point where we got stuck. And he has responded with modifications, again as a short Lean file with various axioms as placeholders. Such a dialogue is still ongoing. I don't know whether Mochizuki and his team is doing anything with Lean beyond this at the moment.

@Adam Topaz assuming the critical point remains critical, is your goal to produce a full Lean proof of ABC modulo the critical point? Or a full proof of Corollary 3.12 modulo the critical point? Or just enough Lean to formally state the critical point? Or something like what you mentioned above where a lot of axioms are used to talk about the critical point?

These questions are certainly on our mind, and to some extent the answers are "it depends". But if the critical point is very critical, I personally do not think it is worth spending a lot of effort on formalizing a full proof of ABC modulo that critical point. On the other hand, investments in formalizing prerequisites will also be useful in other projects.

Nevertheless, the nonexistence of a LeanForm in MathLib of ZFC as a first order theory made a strong impression on me, especially considering how fundamental ZFC as a first order theory is throughout pure mathematics

Doubt.
Source.

If the LANA team is implementing species and mutations etc, I'd really, really hope they aren't going to work with isomorphism classes of functors, but the actual 2-categorical structure. In this category theorist's opinion, that single step did an act of violence on what seems to be trying to happen.
Performing the entire IUT project inside a deep embedding of the syntax of ZFC would, I think, make this job much harder than it already is.

For that matter, why not work not in the syntax of ZFC, but in L directly? Does one then get a (hypothetical) proof under the assumption V=L? For abc the statement is simple enough this shouldn't matter, but for eg Corollary 3.12 or other statements that apparently run the risk of upsetting the Foundation axiom? It's late here, and I know this is off-topic for LANA, since it's coming from Mochizuki's plan. Just thinking out loud....

I have many opinions about this, but mathematical discussions should probably take place elsewhere (e.g. in #maths ). As for the question of whether LANA is using a deep embedding of ZFC, the answer so far is “no”.

Update:
LANA Project Interim Report 2026: Computer-Assisted Verification of IUT Theory - YouTube
https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=KADN5NHmIfw
Is the existence of the S displayed at minute 40:30 of this video expected (by skeptics of IUT) to be (a) true, but as hard to prove as abc is to prove, or (b) false?

@Adam Topaz @Johan Commelin I listened to this today (while doing some errands). It was really interesting. My understanding (possibly wrong) is that you got the ABC conjecture claimed “proof” narrowed down to a particular unproven equality, ηq=ηSanab\eta_q = \eta_S^\textrm{anab}ηq​=ηSanab​ (40:30 in video), and that is the missing piece. Mochizuki claims it is obvious (or some synonym of obvious), but you can’t seem to figure out how to prove it. But it is different from the Scholze and Stix analysis and in particular you feel Scholze and Stix had a misunderstanding of the proof, so their critism doesn’t hold for this equality.

  1. Is this correct, or am I missing something?
  2. Is the main missing equality formalized in Lean (statement, not proof), to make it clear what it is?
  3. Are you fairly confident the rest of ABC would follow from that missing equality (even if you haven’t formalized all of it)?
  4. How has Mochizuki responded? Is he willing to try to flesh out that missing part? Does he still think it is obvious?
  5. Have Scholze or Stix had a chance to respond to this development?
  6. Do you conjecture the missing equality is true? (I think you answered yes to that given the emoji on the previous message).
  7. Do you conjecture that the missing equality is exceptionally challenging to prove, so might not be that helpful to finishing ABC? (Again, I think from the last message the answer is yes, but it might depend on how skeptical one is of IUT as Timothy put it.)
  8. Will you submit your findings for peer reviewed publication?
  9. How do you feel about this? Do you feel this has provided clarity, or we are still where we were pre-LANA?

I just read the LANA Report today. I don't claim to understand the math, but I can understand this:

Already here, the problem that would later be called the “wall” inside LANA appeared... At this point, it was not clear whether this was simply a lack of understanding on the LANA side, or whether it was a problem related to the argument of the paper itself. (pg. 4)

and also this:

the concept of a “link” needs a more precise definition that can be formalized in Lean. (pg. 42)

Certainly, IUT is not the only theory that is "too ambiguous to be formalized"--many people I know who have formalized their own papers have discovered holes in their argument; definitions that need clarification.

To me, this is exactly the purpose of formalization: to make things precise. Hopefully, the IUT experts can see that even if LANA gives a negative result, this level of scrutiny is in fact a very good thing for their field in the long term.

Thanks for the questions and comments @Timothy Chow and @Jason Rute -- since Jason's questions include Timothy's let me just respond to those. First, I essentially agree with Jason's summary of the context, except that I don't know whether I would say that Scholze-Stix had a misunderstanding of the proof. Rather, our (LANA) impression is that the key difference between our investigation and what Scholze-Stix did is that we are taking the indeterminacies more seriously than they did. In this sense, we are trying to go quite further than they did, but we don't necessarily disagree with the content of their report! Let me now address the questions one by one:

  1. See above.
  2. We don't have a complete formalization of the statement of this equality, but the point is that we are certain that it can be formalized. (We do have a formalization of most of the objects involved modulo "standard" constructions/theorems as axioms, and could probably formalize the statement of this equality relatively easily.)
  3. Yes.
  4. Mochizuki hasn't yet responded directly to this report, however we have been in contact with him over the last few weeks, so I don't think any of what we said in the press conference will come as a surprise to him. What I can say is that Mochizuki and the group at RIMS has been working on reformulating the argument to make it amenable to formalization. We don't yet know how this will turn out.
  5. We haven't discussed with them beforehand.
  6. As far as I am concerned, conjecturing whether or not this equality is true is not the job of the LANA group. Rather, our job is to faithfully encode IUT into Lean, and Lean will tell us whether or not the proof works. The main barrier now is that we don't know how to encode the argument of the ηq=ηSanab\eta_q = \eta_S^{anab}ηq​=ηSanab​ into Lean.
  7. See my answer to 6.
  8. We don't have any such plans at the moment. This will likely change once we reach a final conclusion to the project overall.
  9. I'm quite happy that we are able to provide a precise mathematical assertion, and a statement that can be formalized, from which Corollary 3.12 follows directly. However, we feel that the way the argument is presented in the original IUT papers cannot be formalized as is, which is frustrating as this means we're stuck. However, the argument is now evolving in the sense that Mochizuki is reformulating various aspects of the argument, which is why our project still hasn't reached a final conclusion.

I didn't watch the video so sorry if this is explained: are you saying that Scholze and Stix concerns are resolved/formalized or that you are following a different strategy that ignores their main objection (or something else)?
The link in @Jack McCarthy is invalid. The correct link is this probably https://github.com/katobungen/LANA_report_202607/blob/pdf/LANA_report_202607.pdf
Oh, I see that my question has an answer in the pdf.

The Scholze/Stix concerns are not resolved. Their concerns are not explicitly formalized but it is also not accurate to say that the LANA effort "ignores their main objection." The main objection/concern has always been that people don't understand how Corollary 3.12 follows from what has been established up to that point. There are different ways to say "I don't understand how to get from A to B." You might say, "I see how to get from A to A' and I see how to get from B' to B but I don't see how to get from A' to B'." Or you might say, "If by A you mean A* and if by B you mean B* then B* definitely doesn't follow from A*." The former is perhaps more like what LANA is saying and the latter is perhaps more like what Scholze and Stix are saying. But the bottom line is still, "I don't see how to get from A to B."

I can understand how LANA wants to maintain a neutral position on whether a suitable S is likely to exist. If we want an opinion on the matter then we'd probably have to drag in someone like Scholze or Stix (I say "drag in" because they're surely sick of the controversy and would prefer not to have to waste more of their time on it). The reason I asked is that whether S is likely to exist or not may illuminate what role we can expect Lean to play in this story. If S is likely to exist then maybe one could formally prove that the existence of S is equivalent to abc. If S is likely not to exist then maybe the Scholze-Stix argument can be used to give a formal proof of a weaker nonexistence statement.

I'm excited to see LANA's code when/if it is made public. AFAIK neither LANA nor Mochizuki's team have produced any formal artifacts yet, only informal progress reports. Do we have an approximate timeline for when we might have this?

As a small piece of feedback, I am mildly disappointed to see the LANA document use the ..."poetic" language of the IUT as a matter of course, rather than using only rigorous terminology (modulo the imprecision of "harmless simplification", and standard abus de langage) and explaining which definitions correspond to the more vague statements (what is a "ring theoretic environment" and how does an abstract topological group belong to one, for instance? Why not say "there is a functor Ring -> TopGrp such that etc etc"?) I appreciate there are many authors, but I have read so much of Mochizuki I now feel allergic to his phrasing and quite frankly waffly terminology. The definitions in Lean that I presume the team has are not vague, cannot they be translated not back to Mochizukisms, but to standard mathematical terminology, except where they are wholly original terms for rigorous structures?

I will say that I am however very happy to see this document, and hope the team can give further clarifications as they arise. I appreciate that it can have been painstaking (and perhaps painful) work to get even this far, and my utmost respect for the people working on LANA.

To put it more simply, but more boldly: a deformalisation into standard terminology of what mathematics is done in Lean, or at least to ready-to-formalise-quality, is to me much more valuable than adhering to the IUT paper terminology. But this is just my personal wishlist, though I think you'd be hard-pressed to find someone who would disagree that a direct translation of the lean code to standard natural-language 'spelling' is useful.

Adhering to Mochizuki's language as closely to possible makes total sense to me, because otherwise LANA runs the risk of being accused by Mochizuki of misformalization (in the scenario where a proof of abc does not materialize; of course if abc is formally proved then this matters less). There will be time enough later for translation into "standard" mathematical language for anyone who wants to see that.

I didn't say to excise his language completely. I think a dictionary to say what his phrases mean is surely going to happen, but for Mochizuki-natural-language:Lean. There's no reason to not then subsequently extend this translation to then be Lean:idiomatic-natural-langauge.

But attempting to explain to the general (mathematical) public what his words are supposed to actually mean by repeating his phrases is like just "shouting English louder at foreigners" (if you'll pardon the phrase)

All that is fine, but I think LANA is taking a "first things first" approach, which I think is wise. The first order of business is to bend over backwards to try to resolve the controversy. Other desiderata can be addressed later.

Timothy Chow said:

The first order of business is to bend over backwards to try to resolve the controversy.

Why? As long as Mochizuki refuses to acknowledge gaps in his proof, there will be controversy. Controversy is a natural part of any scientific endeavor. I agree with @David Michael Roberts that I would prefer to read clear, precise mathematical arguments even if that upsets the Mochizuki camp.

Re: controversy, I think we have seen that this project (although the LANA group would know better) has made Mochizuki more open to dialog. I imagine it is both LANA’s willingness to engage with his proof in good faith (even if it is more deferential than some might like) and the use of Lean as a precise communication tool to avoid misunderstanding and ambiguity. At least the value of Lean in getting Mochizuki to engage is documented in the thread above, including Adam’s remark that Mochizuki is reworking the proof to be easier to formalize.

Jack McCarthy said:

Controversy is a natural part of any scientific endeavor.

I don't agree that controversy is a natural feature of mathematics. In fact, I'd say that one thing that distinguishes mathematics from every other field of academic study is its stunningly low rate of controversies of this type. Endless controversies (where both parties are in the mathematical establishment) are outliers, and the Mochizuki situation is an outlier among outliers.

Even total laymen have raised the possibility of ITPs resolving the controversy over abc. Of course, there was one thing the laymen didn't understand: a resolution is possible only if the person claiming to have a proof respects the ITP. In the early days, Mochizuki did not realize how far ITPs had come, and still thought of as computers as useful tools for routine calculation, incapable of verifying advanced mathematics. Now that Mochizuki himself understands the capabilities of Lean, the opportunity for a resolution has suddenly materialized. I applaud the LANA team for doing their utmost to not squander this opportunity.

Of course, there remains the possibility that the gap in the formal proof cannot be filled, yet Mochizuki "flips" and declares that Lean isn't so capable after all. "A crank is a crank is a crank," the skeptic may say. But again, I don't think that this is a given. Someone recently pointed out to me that Craig Feinstein, who barely understands any mathematics, was persuaded by his experience with Isabelle/HOL that he doesn't have a proof of P ≠ NP. If an ITP can change the mind of even someone like Craig Feinstein, then I don't see why we can't expect a successful resolution to the Mochizuki controversy. At the very least, I think we should try, rather than shrug our shoulders and and say that controversy in mathematics is just as "natural" as in, say, religion or politics.

Perhaps there are not endless controversies about correctness, but there are certainly many endless controversies about language, notations, and explanations. We see them very often in this Zulip regarding the "canonical" way to formalize a statement--everyone has different ideas of how things ought to be defined.

The point David raised was not about the correctness of Mochizuki's work, but about his use of non-standard, imprecise, waffly terminology. That is an issue that can not be resolved by an ITP because it is subjective.

The concern is not whether Mochizuki will ever admit he doesn't have a proof--but whether he will force all future students of IUT to conform to his poor choice of language.

I can live with the deference to raise the level of engagement. But reusing turns of phrase as part of explanations meant to clarify, when the original use of those phrases was also not helpful in clarifying, is nothing to do with misformalisation. This isn't rewriting definitions, but changing the expository text to only use standard (or otherwise rigorous) terms everywhere possible.

I very much welcome the efforts in Kyoto to rewrite the source material to make it more transparent, and my long-held position is that the IUT papers should have been rewritten to be clearer years ago, not just tinkered with, nor hundreds of pages of metaphor ("/\ vs \/" screeds etc) produced that was not clarifying for the mathematics.

I will reiterate my respect for the team going through this process, I only want this to be seen as feedback as to how the explanatory power of their outputs could be increased.
I would actually like to discuss the mathematical content of this report, but I appreciate this is not Lean-related and so this forum is not the place to do it. Anyone who would like to please DM me

I still maintain that this is putting the cart before the horse. If the controversy is not resolved, or if it is resolved in the negative direction (i.e., Mochizuki is wrong), then IUT is going to remain a sideshow of little interest except to a few specialists, and so I don't think it matters too much whether the terminology is optimized. If it is resolved in the positive direction and abc is proved, then the larger mathematical community is going to swarm all over it, and all these details will quickly be repaired. And the only possible way this final outcome will materialize is if Mochizuki really does have a proof and is coaxed into giving a lot more details than he has given to date.

I still hold out hope that the techniques might ultimately prove useful for something, regardless of the outcome of the abc conjecture here, and getting terminology clear and rigorous matters a lot for usability. If Mochizuki wants people to actually adopt his ideas, using vagueries will actively hurt that aim.

I’m very much a non-expert here, but I came across this video and became curious whether there are plans to engage with Kirti Joshi’s comments on the LANA project.

Given that LANA has narrowed the difficulty to a fairly specific point in the passage from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12, and Kirti Joshi argues that his own framework addresses the relevant issue, are there any plans to try formalizing Joshi's proposed route in Lean?

It seems that even a limited formalization of the constructions he proposes could help clarify whether they actually overcome the obstruction LANA has isolated. Or is the LANA project’s scope solely to reconstruct Mochizuki’s original argument?

/cc @Adam Topaz @Johan Commelin
No, we have no such plans, primarily because there is no analogous controversy, please refer to this mathoverflow thread.
Joshi is of course welcome to formalize his own proof.

Adam Topaz said:

Joshi is of course welcome to formalize his own proof.

Given the recent success of autoformalizing FLT, perhaps it won't be long before he has realistic means to do so, or someone else points a powerful agent at his papers for him.

Harald Husum said:

Given the recent success of autoformalizing FLT, perhaps it won't be long before he has realistic means to do so, or someone else points a powerful agent at his papers for him.

That's assuming he has a proof, but in a rare moment of agreement, both Scholze and Mochizuki agree that he doesn't.
Given the successful story on N-S equation, is it possible to ask AI to fill in the gaps in IUT theory? Of course the token cost will be huge.

I really meant to say that he will have means to attempt to do so. I wasn't claiming I am particularly confident that he has a proof. That is above my pay grade.

I do think we'll get to a point where a serious and well executed attempt at autofomalization will be enough to settle the question pretty convincingly, whether successful or not. I don't know of any serious results in anabelian geometry has been autoformalized, so we're not there yet. But once AI agents have amassed a strong portfolio of such formalizations, having the same agents fail at formalizing a given proof would say quite a bit about that proof. Particularly if the agents point to a particular argument as unsound and not easily fixable.

Jz Pan said:

Given the successful story on N-S equation, is it possible to ask AI to fill in the gaps in IUT theory? Of course the token cost will be huge.

You can ask, but it won't succeed. The hoped-for success story here is that Mochizuki will finally admit that he's wrong. That will demonstrate that ITPs have the ability to persuade people that they're wrong, when all the human experts in the world (for social reasons) cannot.
